the risk of developing upper extremity symptoms or functional impairment among workers in new jobs is not associated with the job demands or the physical and psychosocial work environment, but is associated with the physical workload and the psychosocial work demands of the previous job.

the prevalence of upper extremity disorders is high among workers who have been employed for 6 or more months in their present jobs, and that this prevalence is higher among those who have had previous upper extremity problems than among those who have not.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the physical and psychosocial work environment, and the development of musculoskeletal disorders in the workplace.
the prediction of upper extremity (UE) symptoms and functional impairment (FI) among workers employed for six months in a new occupation.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is insufficient evidence to support a causal relationship between work-related upper extremity musculoskeletal disorders and work.

the most important predictors of work disability are not the individual factors such as age, gender and education, but rather the social factors such as the economic situation, the work environment and social security.
there are no clear-cut predictors of upper extremity (UE) symptoms and functional impairment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the results suggest a need for further studies of the relationship between the job demands, the job control and upper extremity symptoms, as well as the role of psychosocial factors and the development of symptoms.
we have found a high prevalence of work related upper extremity symptoms among workers in new jobs.
the more the job requires the use of upper extremities (UE) and the more repetitive the work, the more likely the worker would develop symptoms and functional impairment.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have identified a number of risk factors for the development of work-related upper extremity pain and functional limitations in a population of workers with less than 6 months of tenure in a new job.
the majority of workers with new upper extremity symptoms in a new job are not at risk for developing persistent upper extremity disorders (UEDs).
the majority of the population has a high risk for developing upper extremity symptoms in the workplace.
